## Executive summary Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in ASP.NET Core SignalR (Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime). This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability. A denial of service vulnerability exists in ASP.NET Core SignalR in .NET 8, .NET 9, and .NET 10. Stateful reconnect can be leveraged by an attacker to deny service to other users. ## Discussion Discussion for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/67787 ## CVSS Details - **Version:** 3.1 - **Severity:** High - **Score:** 7.5 - **Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H/E:U/RL:O/RC:C` - **Weakness:** CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling) ## Affected Platforms - **Platforms:** All - **Architectures:** All ### Mitigation Factors Your ASP.NET Core app is only affected if it uses SignalR with stateful reconnect enabled. ## Affected Packages The vulnerability affects any Microsoft .NET project if it uses any of affected package versions listed below ### .NET 10.0 Package name | Affected version | Patched version ------------ | ---------------- | ------------------------- [Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.linux-arm](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.linux-arm) | >= [Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.osx-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.osx-x64) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.25 | 8.0.26 [Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.win-x64](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.win-x64) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.25 | 8.0.26 [Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.win-x86](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App.Runtime.win-x86) | >= 8.0.0, <= 8.0.25 | 8.0.26 ## Advisory FAQ ### How do I know if I am affected? If using a package listed in [affected packages](#affected-packages), you're exposed to the vulnerability. ### How do I fix the issue? 1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs. 2. If your application references the vulnerable nuget package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the `dotnet --info` command. * If you're using .NET 8.0, you should download and install .NET 8.0.29 Runtime or .NET 8.0.129 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/8.0. * If you're using .NET 9.0, you should download and install .NET 9.0.18 Runtime or .NET 9.0.316 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/9.0. * If you're using .NET 10.0, you should download and install .NET 10.0.10 Runtime or .NET 10.0.302 SDK from https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-core/10.0. Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect. Additionally, if you've deployed [self-contained applications](https://docs.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/deploying/#self-contained-deployments-scd) targeting any of the impacted versions, these applications are also vulnerable and must be recompiled and redeployed. ## Other Information ### Reporting Security Issues If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the [MSRC Researcher Portal](https://msrc.microsoft.com/report/vulnerability/new). Further information can be found in the MSRC [Report an Issue FAQ](https://www.microsoft.com/msrc/faqs-report-an-issue). Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty. ### Support You can ask questions about this issue on GitHub in the .NET GitHub organization. The main repos are located at https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore. The Announcements repo (https://github.com/dotnet/Announcements) will contain this bulletin as an issue and will include a link to a discussion issue. You can ask questions in the linked discussion issue. ### Disclaimer The information provided in this advisory is provided "as is" without warranty of any kind. Some states do not allow the exclusion or limitation of liability for consequential or incidental damages so the foregoing limitation may not apply. ### External Links [CVE-2026-56170]( https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-56170) ### Acknowledgements Ky0toFu ### Revisions V1.0 (July 14, 2026): Advisory published.

Issues.Title: [release/3.1] Reset current_no_gc_region_info after leaving no gc region implicitly
Issues.Body:
Backport https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/73602.

## Customer Impact
Customers reported occasional `System.InvalidOperationException` with message `The NoGCRegion mode was already in progress` when calling `GC.TryStartNoGCRegion`. This is preventing them from using this optimization and impacting their cold start latencies.

## Testing
Customers have tried the fix on .NET 6 overnight and reported the exception never appears again. Meanwhile, there is an unpatched machine and observed 72 exceptions of the same type in the same time interval, proving this does fix the bug.

## Risk
Low. This only impact customer using `TryStartNoGCRegion`, and this is the right thing to do.

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/coreclr) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Migrate FabricBot Tasks to Config-as-Code
Issues.Body:
**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/cli) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/cli) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. If you have any questions or concerns with this pull request, please contact [MerlinBot Expert DRI](mailto:merlinbotdri@microsoft.com).

Issues.Title: Confusing behavior when using AssemblyInfo.cs
Issues.Body:
I'm completely perplexed.

I created a .Net Standard 2.0 library project.

I explicity added an AssemblyInfo.cs file, we need this because we use this utility to "stamp" our assemblies when we build them:

https://github.com/ygoe/NetRevisionTool

That utility is run as a pre/post build event and temporarily replaces placeholders in the AssemblyInformationalVersion attribute with runtime values (like repo folder name, commit ID, branch etc etc).

The completed assembly then has this info "burned" into it as we go forward.

.Net Standard is not working with this.

1. It seems to populatethe Package Version (in the project's Package section) with whatever we put into AssemblyInfo.cs for AssemblyInformationalVersion.
2. The version of the generated nuget package is always set as 1.0.0.

This is just mind blowing, is there no way we can do this seemingly simple operation any more if adopt .Net Standard?

Issues.Title: Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions
Issues.Body:
I was looking through this repository to determine if .NET Standard 2.1 libraries support default interface methods - it looks like they do, given the presence of `System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.DefaultImplementationsOfInterfaces`, as well as my own experimenting in VS 2019. It seems I was mistaken when thinking that this was not the case, so I'm glad this repository is easily accessible to determine this.

But while doing this, I found it difficult to determine what commits were included in this particular .NET Standard version. I see that there's a tag `v2.1.0-prerelease.19126.1`, as well as branches `release/2.0.0`, `release/3.0`, and `release/3.0-preview9`. One of the machines I tested VS 2019 on had a `netstandard.dll` assembly, itself targeting .NETStandard v2.1.0, with AssemblyInformationalVersion `1.1.0+a5b5f2e1e369972c8ff1e2183979fab6099f52ef`; this commit is part of the `release/3.0` branch. However, another machine had a same-named assembly, targeting .NETCoreApp v3.0 and AssemblyInformationalVersion `3.0.0+4ac4c0367003fe3973a3648eb0715ddb0e3bbcea`, and I don't see that commit hash in this repository.

Additionally, [this blog post](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/the-future-of-net-standard/) states that 2.1 will be the last version, but there is another prerelease tag `v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1` and [on GitHub](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/releases/tag/v2.2.0-prerelease.19564.1) it's labelled .NET 5.0 Preview 2.

So I have a few questions for understanding this repository:

1. Since .NET Standard 2.1 is released, are there plans to continue development in this repository for e.g. the shared BCL going forward with .NET 5+?
2. Are there multiple kinds of `netstandard.dll` for a single .NET Standard version? E.g. are there separate versions for .NET Framework to reference and for .NET Core / .NET 5+ to reference?
3. Do the tags / branch names in this repository correspond to a .NET Standard version or something else?
4. It looks like there are patch releases; are there patch versions of a single .NET Standard version?
5. Are there other repositories which are being used to create `netstandard.dll`?
6. Is there a way to determine, from the repository, which commit is the one used for a given release?

Thank you for your consideration.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Questions about tagging within this repository / future versions" (#1777)

Issues.Title: Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1
Issues.Body:
# Summary

.NET Standard version is not resolved correctly when a transitive dependency targets multiple .NET Standard versions.

# Environment

- Windows 10 (19042.746)
- .NET 5 SDK 5.0.201

# Minimal reproducible example
[bug.zip](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/files/6209239/bug.zip)

This is a three-project solution:
- `TestProject1` targeting `netcoreapp3.1`
- `ClassProject1` targeting `netstandard2.0`
- `ClassProject2` targeting *both* `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1`

The project dependency chain is: `TestProject1 -> ClassProject1 -> ClassProject2`

A method (`ClassProject2Test1`) on `ClassProject2` is hidden behind a `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.

# The issue

The unit test failed with a `MissingMethodException`

```
[xUnit.net 00:00:00.38]     TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [FAIL]
  Failed TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1 [2 ms]
  Error Message:
   System.MissingMethodException : Method not found: 'Void ClassLibrary2.Class2.Class2Test1()'.
  Stack Trace:
     at ClassLibrary1.Class1.Class1Test1()
   at TestProject1.UnitTest1.Test1() in C:\Users\rex\source\netstandard-bug-repro\TestProject1\UnitTest1.cs:line 12
```

# Expected result

The compiler should have resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.0)*` 

# Actual result

The compiler resolved the chain as:

`TestProject1 (.NET Core 3.1) -> ClassProject1 (.NET Standard 2.0) -> *ClassProject2 (.NET Standard 2.1)*` 

Which causes the exception because the offending method, `ClassProject2Test1`, was hidden by the `#if NETSTANDARD2_0` preprocessor directive.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Issue with resolving between .NET Standard 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1" (#1787)

Issues.Title: Security Vulnerability due to System.Text.RegularExpressions
Issues.Body:
### Problem
There is a security vulnerability with the version of System.Text.RegularExpressions that is used by dotnet standard. The vulnerable version of System.Text.RegularExpressions is 4.3.0. Please see links below for the vulnerability documentation or discussion:

https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/en-US/vulnerability/CVE-2019-0820
https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/111
https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2019-0820
https://snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-DOTNET-SYSTEMTEXTREGULAREXPRESSIONS-174708
https://www.whitesourcesoftware.com/vulnerability-database/CVE-2019-0820

The dotnet commit that fixed the vulnerability is https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/commit/19d4b1163d8a03dd90ff5fd1785eea6305112545

### Issue:
We use whitesource and it has caught this issue with high severity. We don't consume System.Text.RegularExpressions directly but packages that use this. Therefore as a transitive dependency due to NetStandard library, which is being used by several other dotnet packages like Castle Windsor, MassTransit etc., Once an update is available the others could followup and update.

### Code:

[The latest version 2.0.3 of Net standard ](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) still seem to be using System.Text.RegularExpressions version 4.3.0 as per https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/src/apicompat/netstandard/netstandard.depproj

### Fix
Please update[ library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/NETStandard.Library/) targeting .netStandard 1.6 to update System.Text.RegularExpression package to latest secured version 4.3.1 to fix the security issue or kindly suggest alternatives.

Issues.Title: System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings slow
Issues.Body:
_This issue has been moved from [a ticket on Developer Community](https://developercommunity2.visualstudio.com/t/SystemDrawingPrintingPrinterSettings-/890524)._ --- Hello I'm debugging a problem with the printer settings. Some calls are significant slower if the default printer is a network printer, even if I explicit set a local printer name. After studying referencesource I think I found the culprit. I call: var printerSettings = new System.Drawing.Printing.PrinterSettings(); printerSettings.PrinterName = "LOCALPRINTER"; // the next call is slow if the OS default printer is a network printer var res = printerSettings.DefaultPageSettings.PrinterResolution Internally FastDeviceCapabilities is called. FastDeviceCapabilities calls GetOutputPort. But GetOutput port return the port of the default printer and not the port of the given printer! In addition, DeviceCapabilities is then called with a wrong combination of printer name and port, don't know if this could lead to additional problems. Resolution: GetOutputPort should return the port of the given printer and not accessing the default printer at all. Issues.Title: Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF
Issues.Body:
I'm working on converting a large WPF solution's projects to SDK style and ran into some issues.

The solution is large with multiple projects(old style) all targeting .net452 and some nugets(some made by me) installed, targeting both .net452 and .netstandard2.1 This all seems to work fine, somehow the nuget manages to install the correct version targeting .net452.

I have decided to slowly convert the projects inside the solution to SDK style targeting .net452 and .netstandard2.1 just like the nugets.

This is where the problem starts, one project was converted so far that is referenced by multiple other projects. Localy everything seems to build and run fine, however when Azure DevOps(VS version 2019) is used to build the solution there are 2 scenarios:

1. The famous error message is shown:

                "Error CS0012: The type 'Object' is defined in an assembly that is not referenced. You must add a reference to assembly 
                 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0"

2. It builds fine but on app launch it crashes with:

                 "Could not load file or assembly 'netstandard, Version=2.1.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' 
                 or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified."

I'm suspecting that the problem is related to referencing the SDK project, it looks like that somehow it references the .netstandard2.1 instead of the .net452.

The reason this is my suspicion is that if targetframework is set to only .net452 on the referenced project everything works fine. Google has led me to two possible solutions to tell the project what framework to use from the reference:

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj"
                  AdditionalProperties="TargetFramework=net452">
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
and

```
<ProjectReference Include="..\..\..\..\foo\foo.csproj">
      <SetTargetFramework>TargetFramework=net452</SetTargetFramework>
      <Project>{xxxxxx-xxxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxx-xxxxxxx}</Project>
      <<Name>foo</Name>
</ProjectReference>
```
This doesn't look like it's doing anything and the problem still persists. At the moment I ran out of ideas and I'm here asking for help. Please let me know what I'm doing wrong or what else I can try.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Build issues when referencing project that targets multiple frameworks C# WPF" (#1776)

**TL;DR;** Requesting to add [FabricBot](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/fabricbot_overview) configuration associated with your repository to `.github/fabricbot.json`.

**Context**

FabricBot is now a [config-as-code-only](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/bot-config-as-code) platform. As a result, while you can still use the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) to modify your FabricBot configuration, you can no longer save the changes. The only way to save changes to your configuration at the moment is to _export configuration_ from the portal and upload the exported configuration to `.github/fabricbot.json` in your repository. In this pull request, we are adding your FabricBot configuration to your repository at `.github/fabricbot.json` so that you can make changes to it going forward.

While the [FabricBot Configuration Portal](https://portal.fabricbot.ms/bot/?repo=dotnet/corefx) is the *only way* to modify your FabricBot configuration at the moment, we have a feature on our backlog to publish the JSON schema defining the structure of the FabricBot configuration file. With the JSON schema, you can (1) use a plaintext editor of your choice to modify the FabricBot configuration file and use the schema to validate the file after editing or (2) [configure](https://code.visualstudio.com/Docs/languages/json#_json-schemas-and-settings) VS Code to use the schema when editing FabricBot configuration file to take advantage of convenience features such as automatic code completion and field description on mouseover.

[*Pull Request Create*](https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot/extensions/prcreate), a [MerlinBot](https://https://eng.ms/docs/products/1es-data-insights/merlinbot) Extension, was used to automatically create this pull request. Issues.Title: Fix RSA OAEP decryption in OpenSSL with non-power-of-two keys lengths
Issues.Body:
## Customer Impact

A customer reported in dotnet/runtime#71607 that decrypting RSA OAEP with SHA2 and a 3072-bit key on Linux resulted in a OAEP de-padding error, while other platforms were able to perform these operations successfully.

Investigation in to the issue led to uncover that RSA OAEP decryption that uses the managed implementation does not work with non-power-of-two keys because we do not slice a rented buffer accordingly. The current implementation only works because `CryptoPool.Rent` happens to give back power-of-two arrays which are exactly the same size as the key.

The fix is to slice the data to the correct size.

This does not affect dotnet/runtime because the managed implementation of RSA OAEP is no longer used for OpenSSL RSA decryption. This change was introduced in dotnet/runtime#50063.

## Testing

Unit tests were introduced to test RSA OAEP encryption with a 3072-bit RSA key. These tests will be forward-ported to dotnet/runtime.

## Risk

Minimal. The change is localized and understood that a `Slice` was missing.

Issues.Body:
Moves the `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.ExternalAccess.Extensions` implementation into the unified `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Features.ExternalAccess` assembly, following the source-move/type-forwarding pattern established in #81593. The old Extensions assembly becomes a thin compatibility façade.

## Implementation moves

- **Source + resources** — All 7 `.cs` files, `ExternalAccessExtensionsResources.resx`, and 13 `.xlf` files relocated from `src/Features/ExternalAccess/Extensions/` to `src/Features/ExternalAccess/Core/Extensions/` (preserving the `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Extensions` namespace)

## Core EA project (`Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Features.ExternalAccess`)

Issues.Title: Workspace APIs unusable on Blazor WebAssembly under .NET 11: AddProject takes a blocking SemaphoreSlim.Wait
Issues.Body:
**Version Used**: `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Workspaces` 5.3.0 (also reproduces on 5.6.0)

Minimal repro: https://github.com/SimonCropp/roslyn-wasm-blocking-wait

## Summary

`AdhocWorkspace.AddProject` throws `PlatformNotSupportedException` on single-threaded Blazor WebAssembly under .NET 11. The same call, with the same Roslyn version, succeeds on .NET 10. Since `AddProject` is the entry point to every workspace scenario, this means no Roslyn workspace can be constructed on browser-wasm at all under .NET 11.

## Steps to Reproduce

Adding one empty project is enough — no documents, no compilation, no completion:

```csharp
var workspace = new AdhocWorkspace();
workspace.AddProject(ProjectInfo.Create(
    ProjectId.CreateNewId(), VersionStamp.Default, "Probe", "Probe", LanguageNames.CSharp));
```

The repro is two Blazor WebAssembly projects with `Workspace.cs` and `BlazorMain.cs` linked into both, so the code under test is byte-identical and the target framework is the only difference:

| Project | TFM | Roslyn | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Net10` | net10.0 | 5.3.0 | AddProject succeeds |
| `Net11` | net11.0 | 5.3.0 | **`PlatformNotSupportedException`** |

```
dotnet run --project Net11/Net11.csproj
```

## Expected Behavior

`AddProject` succeeds, as it does on .NET 10.

## Actual Behavior

```
System.PlatformNotSupportedException: Arg_PlatformNotSupported
   at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.RuntimeFeature.ThrowIfMultithreadingIsNotSupported()
   at System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim.WaitCore(Int64 millisecondsTimeout, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim.Wait(CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Roslyn.Utilities.SemaphoreSlimExtensions.DisposableWait(SemaphoreSlim semaphore, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.ProjectDependencyGraph.GetProjectsThatTransitivelyDependOnThisProject(ProjectId projectId)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.SolutionCompilationState.AddProjects(ArrayBuilder`1 projectInfos)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Solution.AddProjects(ArrayBuilder`1 projectInfos)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Solution.AddProject(ProjectInfo projectInfo)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspace.CheckAndAddProject(Solution newSolution, ProjectInfo project)
   ...
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.Workspace.OnProjectAdded(ProjectInfo projectInfo)
   at Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.AdhocWorkspace.AddProject(ProjectInfo projectInfo)
```

## What changed on the runtime side

`SemaphoreSlim.WaitCore` gained an unconditional multithreading check in .NET 11.

release/10.0 — guarded, so it only applied to the threaded wasm build:

```csharp
CheckDispose();
#if FEATURE_WASM_MANAGED_THREADS
    Thread.AssureBlockingPossible();
#endif
```

main — unconditional, so it now also fires in the single-threaded build that Blazor WebAssembly uses by default:

```csharp
RuntimeFeature.ThrowIfMultithreadingIsNotSupported();
```

To be fair to the runtime side: `SemaphoreSlim.Wait` and `WaitCore` carry `[UnsupportedOSPlatform("browser")]` in release/10.0 too. That annotation is not new, so .NET 10 was not offering a supported guarantee — it simply never enforced the restriction outside the threaded build, and code taking an uncontended wait kept working.

That is why I am raising this here rather than only against the runtime: Roslyn is calling an API annotated unsupported-on-browser, on a path that browser-hosted callers cannot avoid.

## Question

Is it feasible for `ProjectDependencyGraph.GetProjectsThatTransitivelyDependOnThisProject` (and the `SetCurrentSolution` path that reaches it) to avoid a blocking `SemaphoreSlim.Wait`? The wait appears to be uncontended in the single-threaded case — it never actually blocks, which is precisely why this worked on .NET 10.

The documented alternative of enabling `WasmEnableThreads`, which would satisfy the runtime check, is not currently viable either: the .NET 11 runtime fails to start with threads enabled — dotnet/runtime#131311 (repro: https://github.com/SimonCropp/wasm-threads-startup-crash).

## Context

The affected app is the in-browser query explorer in [Scry](https://github.com/Papyrine/Scry), which hosts Roslyn in Blazor WebAssembly for completion over a synthesized query model. It works on .NET 10 and cannot initialize on .NET 11.

Environment: SDK 11.0.100-preview.6.26359.118, runtimes 11.0.0-preview.6.26359.118 and 10.0.9, Windows 11 x64, Chromium 148. Only .NET 11 preview 6 was tested; it is the latest published preview at time of writing.

Issues.Title: Run Razor decl C# lowering before tag-helper discovery (classify-first component split)
Issues.Body:
### What

Reorder the Razor engine phases so a component's markup split and **decl C# lowering run before tag-helper discovery**, and rewrite the split to partition the *classified* class body. The decl half — the markup-free tag-helper-descriptor surface (base type, interfaces, type parameters, parameters/fields/methods) — is produced from user source alone, independent of tag-helper resolution. The markup-bearing impl half (the render method plus any markup-bearing methods) flows through the rest of the pipeline.

Every component now splits: a markup-free `@code` sends its whole body to the decl half; only a component the analysis can't route safely (a markup property, `@inject`, a preprocessor directive, a header/arity directive combined with markup, or unrecoverable syntax) falls back to a single document.

### Why

The resolution-independent decl half is the enabler for the Sonic incremental source generator: a follow-up feeds it into the SG's input compilation so tag-helper discovery stays incremental without paying for full tag-helper resolution per keystroke. This PR establishes the classify-first pipeline that produces the decl early; it does not yet consume it.

### Commits

1. **Add decl-half baselines to the integration-test harness** — a `DeclDocumentNode` slot and `.decl.ir.txt` / `.decl.codegen.cs` baseline emission, so the partition is reviewable at the IR and C# level. A document with no decl half asserts no decl baseline lingers.
2. **Emit RZ9978 during IR lowering instead of tag-helper discovery** — with discovery moving after IR lowering, the "`@addTagHelper`/`@removeTagHelper`/`@tagHelperPrefix` are not valid in a component" diagnostic is emitted while lowering the directive's `CSharpStatementLiteral`, keyed on the chunk-generator type.
3. **Split the component classify-first: reorder phases and rewrite the split** — the core change (phase reorder in `RazorProjectEngine`, the `DefaultRazorMarkupSplitPhase` rewrite, decl lowering simplification, `MarkupSplitter` tweak, `ComponentWhitespacePass` → optimization). Class-decoration nodes (`@layout`, `@attribute`, `@page`) decorate the decl partial only, so they are never emitted on both halves. The SG's incremental replay restarts at IR lowering on a tag-helper change (rather than at resolution) so that fresh unresolved IR is rebuilt and re-bound — because resolution binds nodes in place, replaying from resolution would find nothing left to rebind.
4. **Remove the superseded impl-derivation fallback** — the split produces the impl half directly, so the final C# lowering always writes the working node; the old `TryWriteImplDocument` path and `IsSplitImplDocument` flag are unreachable and removed.
5. **Regenerate Razor baselines** — derived data (regenerated via `GenerateBaselines`).

### Perf

The decl half is produced but **not yet consumed** (the SG pre-compilation wiring is the follow-up), so this adds a small amount of currently-unused work per component. On an incremental tag-helper change the SG re-lowers the document (as it did before Sonic) — caching the resolution-independent decl across tag-helper changes so it is *not* re-lowered is a deliberate follow-up (the SG pre-compilation rewire), not part of this PR.

### Testing

- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Razor.Language.UnitTests`: green (3901 pass, 2 skipped).
- `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Razor.SourceGenerators.UnitTests`: green (218 pass), including the incremental tag-helper rebinding scenarios.

Issues.Title: Support VB.NET in roslyn-language-server
Issues.Body:
Add support for Visual Basic .NET language in the Roslyn language server. 

Currently the language server supports only C#, but there are various community projects which it seems add VB.NET support by merely recompiling the original roslyn code after adding a few lines of code - for example [vb-ls](https://github.com/CoolCoderSuper/vb-ls) (you can check the two patches [here](https://github.com/CoolCoderSuper/vb-ls/tree/master/vb-ls/patches)) and [roslyn-vbnet-languageserver](https://github.com/LaunchCG/roslyn-vbnet-languageserver).

For my particular use case, this would be useful for exposing VB.NET language server to Copilot CLI (and sometimes VS Code). Currently the only way to use VB.NET language service with Copilot and without untrusted third-party language servers is by using GitHub Copilot in the (full) Visual Studio chat window, which is evolving much slower than Copilot CLI and GitHub Copilot for VS Code.

Issues.Title: Razor cohost ImplementInterface inserts members mid-@code-block with decl/impl split
Issues.Body:
## Summary

On the decl/impl split branch (Sonic), the cohost **ImplementInterface** code action inserts generated interface members in the wrong position within the Razor `@code` block.

## Repro

Test: `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Razor.LanguageClient.Cohost.CodeActions.ImplementInterfaceTests.ImplementInterface_Explicitly_PartialBaseImplementations_AddsDerivedMembers`

A component with `@implements IDerived` and existing explicit `IBase` members in `@code`. Invoking ImplementInterface for `IDerived` inserts the new `IDerived.Property1` / `IDerived.this[]` in the **middle** of the `@code` block (right after `IBase.Property1`) instead of at the end.

- Actual: `IBase.this[]`, `IBase.Property1`, **`IDerived.Property1`, `IDerived.this[]`**, `IBase.Event1`, `IDerived.Event1`
- Expected: `IBase.this[]`, `IBase.Property1`, `IBase.Event1`, **`IDerived.this[]`, `IDerived.Property1`**, `IDerived.Event1`

## Root cause

- The code action runs on the **impl** generated document.
- Roslyn's ImplementInterface groups the new members by kind and inserts each group after the matching existing `IBase` member (`IDerived` property/indexer after `IBase.Property1`; `IDerived.Event1` after `IBase.Event1`).
- The entire `@code` block is emitted under a **single** source mapping (`#line (4,8)-(21,1)` -> `cs[1949..2424] -> razor[46..521]`), so Roslyn's mid-C# insertion maps faithfully to a mid-Razor position.
- Pre-split (single generated document) the layout made Roslyn append everything at the end, so the test passed. Confirmed a decl/impl-split regression by running the test at the pre-split parent commit (passes) vs. the split branch (fails).

## Assessment

An emergent interaction of Roslyn's insertion heuristic, the split's impl-document member layout, and the coarse per-`@code`-block source mapping. A fix likely requires compiler codegen / source-mapping changes or cohost edit post-processing; finer source mappings alone would not help (Roslyn still inserts mid-block). Skipping the test until the decl/impl cohost integration handles this scenario.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Razor cohost ImplementInterface inserts members mid-@code-block with decl/impl split" (#84609)

LDM decision: https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/main/meetings/2026/LDM-2026-07-22.md#allowing-safe-on-non-extern-members.
Relevant speclet section: [`safe` keyword](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/e27fbe625dcb77f81945c38d749b240da0504760/proposals/unsafe-evolution.md#safe-keyword):
>The `safe` modifier can be applied to all declarations which allow `unsafe` to mark them as _requires-unsafe_. It is disallowed to apply both the `safe` and `unsafe` modifier on the same declaration. Like `unsafe` modifier, the `safe` modifier must match on both parts of partial declarations. The compiler requires an explicit `safe` or `unsafe` modifier on [`extern` members](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/e27fbe625dcb77f81945c38d749b240da0504760/proposals/unsafe-evolution.md#extern) and [fields in explicit layout](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/e27fbe625dcb77f81945c38d749b240da0504760/proposals/unsafe-evolution.md#fields). Allowing `safe` even on declarations where it is not required (and hence has no effect for the compiler) is motivated by source generators, e.g., [LibraryImport](https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/blob/e27fbe625dcb77f81945c38d749b240da0504760/proposals/unsafe-evolution.md#answered-allow-safe-on-non-extern-members-libraryimport).
>
>The `safe` modifier only marks the declaration as _not_ _requires-unsafe_, it does not introduce a safe context. There is also no `safe` block or expression form.

Test plan: https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/81207

Issues.Title: Run Razor decl C# lowering before tag-helper discovery (classify-first component split)
Issues.Body:
### What

Reorder the Razor engine phases so a component's markup split and **decl C# lowering run before tag-helper discovery**, and rewrite the split to partition the *classified* class body. The decl half — the markup-free tag-helper-descriptor surface (base type, interfaces, type parameters, parameters/fields/methods) — is produced from user source alone, independent of tag-helper resolution. The markup-bearing impl half (the render method plus any markup-bearing methods) flows through the rest of the pipeline.

Every component now splits: a markup-free `@code` sends its whole body to the decl half; only a component the analysis can't route safely (a markup property, `@inject`, a preprocessor directive, a header/arity directive combined with markup, or unrecoverable syntax) falls back to a single document.

### Why

The resolution-independent decl half is the enabler for the Sonic incremental source generator: a follow-up feeds it into the SG's input compilation so tag-helper discovery stays incremental without paying for full tag-helper resolution per keystroke. This PR establishes the classify-first pipeline that produces the decl early; it does not yet consume it.

### Commits

1. **Add decl-half baselines to the integration-test harness** — a `DeclDocumentNode` slot and `.decl.ir.txt` / `.decl.codegen.cs` baseline emission, so the partition is reviewable at the IR and C# level. A document with no decl half asserts no decl baseline lingers.
2. **Emit RZ9978 during IR lowering instead of tag-helper discovery** — with discovery moving after IR lowering, the "`@addTagHelper`/`@removeTagHelper`/`@tagHelperPrefix` are not valid in a component" diagnostic is emitted while lowering the directive's `CSharpStatementLiteral`, keyed on the chunk-generator type.
3. **Split the component classify-first: reorder phases and rewrite the split** — the core change (phase reorder in `RazorProjectEngine`, the `DefaultRazorMarkupSplitPhase` rewrite, decl lowering simplification, `MarkupSplitter` tweak, `ComponentWhitespacePass` → optimization). Class-decoration nodes (`@layout`, `@attribute`, `@page`) decorate the decl partial only, so they are never emitted on both halves.
4. **Remove the superseded impl-derivation fallback** — the split produces the impl half directly, so the final C# lowering always writes the working node; the old `TryWriteImplDocument` path and `IsSplitImplDocument` flag are unreachable and removed.
5. **Regenerate Razor baselines** — derived data (regenerated via `GenerateBaselines`).

### Perf

The decl half is produced but **not yet consumed** (the SG pre-compilation wiring is the follow-up), so this adds a small amount of currently-unused work per component. The win lands when that wiring consumes the decl.

### Testing / known state

- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Razor.Language.UnitTests`: green (3901 pass, 2 skipped).
- `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Razor.SourceGenerators.UnitTests`: 215 pass, **3 known failures**:
  - `IncrementalCompilation_RazorFiles_WhenProjectReferencesChange`
  - `RazorClassLibrary_Change_Updates_DependentProject_WhenReferencedAsCompilation`
  - `SourceGenerator_CshtmlFiles_NewTagHelper`

  These exercise incremental tag-helper **rebinding**: because discovery now runs after IR lowering, a tag-helper change must re-run discovery + resolution over freshly-lowered IR rather than over already-resolved IR. That rebind is handled by the SG pre-compilation rewire in the follow-up. Non-incremental output is correct — all `CompileToAssembly` tests pass.

Issues.Title: Fix zsh/fish completions emitting invalid Windows-style option switches
Issues.Body:
`dotnet completions script zsh` was emitting Windows-style option aliases (e.g. `/v`, `/verbosity`) as `_arguments` specs, which zsh rejects with:

```
_arguments:comparguments:327: invalid argument: /v=[Set the MSBuild verbosity level...
```

This broke path completions for any command that inherits the verbosity option (e.g. `dotnet build <TAB>`).

## Changes

- **`ZshShellProvider.cs`**: Filter `option.Names()` to only emit names starting with `-` when generating flag and value option specs
- **`FishShellProvider.cs`**: Same filter applied across state walker case patterns, option value completion switches, and completion candidate output — fish also has no concept of `/`-prefixed switches
- **Snapshot updates**: Removed `/v` and `/verbosity` entries from the dotnet CLI zsh snapshot; added new `WindowsStyleAliasesAreFilteredOut` snapshot tests for both shells

The root cause: `CommonOptions.CreateVerbosityOption()` registers `/v` and `/verbosity` as aliases for Windows MSBuild compatibility. Previously all aliases were forwarded verbatim to Unix shell completion specs.

Issues.Title: Design: F# Hot Reload provider shared by dotnet-watch, Visual Studio, and VS Code
Issues.Body:
## Context

[SDK PR #55128](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/55128) is the SDK side of the F# Hot Reload work in [dotnet/fsharp#19941](https://github.com/dotnet/fsharp/pull/19941). Against the corresponding unmerged F# compiler work, it demonstrates F# deltas applied through `dotnet watch`, multiple F# projects in one session, capability changes after process start, and edits in an F# application and referenced F# library. It also contains prototype coordination between Roslyn and F# results, but the PR does not yet contain end-to-end coverage for that mixed-language path.

The current PR is a working prototype, but it has the wrong final boundary. It adds 4,374 lines to the SDK, including a 2,693-line `FSharpHotReloadService` and a separate `FSharpProjectInfo`. That code handles F# project discovery, compiler argument collection, FCS loading and reflection, F# workspace updates, session lifecycle, diagnostics, delta conversion, and part of the mixed-project restart calculation inside `dotnet-watch`.

The [review feedback on #55128](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/55128#issuecomment-5073287244) identified three requirements for the design:

1. Keep the F# footprint in `dotnet-watch` small, with most F# logic supplied by F# components through an explicit host contract.
2. Account for mixed project graphs where C# and F# projects reference each other.
3. Use a design that can also support Visual Studio and the C# Dev Kit path in Visual Studio Code.

This issue is to agree on that design before restructuring #55128.

## Initial delivery scope

The first implementation should target ordinary command-line `dotnet watch`. It should not include Visual Studio, C# Dev Kit, or other editor integration work. The shared-host requirement is a constraint on the contract, not a request to deliver all hosts in the first change.

I also want to minimize churn in the existing Roslyn and watch paths. The first cut should introduce only the neutral contract and coordinator decision needed by `dotnet-watch`, without refactoring unrelated C# and Visual Basic behavior.

The work should be sequenced so the interface and the F# implementation can be reviewed independently:

1. A small contract and coordinator PR that defines the provider result, project and module identity, diagnostics, and prepare, commit, and discard behavior needed for a watch decision. It should use fake providers for its tests and contain no F# compiler implementation.
2. A separate dotnet/fsharp PR that implements that contract over `FSharpHotReloadSession`.
3. A small SDK PR that registers the F# provider for CLI `dotnet watch` and replaces the current prototype bridge.

Visual Studio and C# Dev Kit integration can be separate future work owned and prioritized by those teams. The contract should remain usable there so the CLI implementation does not create a dead-end watch-only API.

## Existing infrastructure

There are several pieces already in place that I think the design should build on.

`dotnet-watch` references [`Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.ExternalAccess.HotReload`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/tree/main/src/Features/ExternalAccess/HotReload). Its [`HotReloadService`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/src/Features/ExternalAccess/HotReload/Api/HotReloadService.cs) owns a solution-wide session and the `StartSession`, `GetUpdates`, `Commit`, `Discard`, and `EndSession` lifecycle.

On current Roslyn main, Visual Studio and C# Dev Kit use the same brokered `ManagedHotReloadLanguageService`. That consolidation was completed in [dotnet/roslyn#82905](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/82905). The debugger-facing contract already has the same session lifecycle and normalized update shape used by the IDE hosts.

Current Roslyn main can represent projects whose compiler it does not own. [dotnet/roslyn#82159](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/82159) added generic loading of projects such as F# to `MSBuildWorkspace`, including their documents, output paths, project references, and metadata references. [dotnet/roslyn#82225](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/82225) uses that information to detect edits in non-Roslyn projects and request rebuild and restart. The remaining Visual Studio synchronization and `CompilationOutputInfo` work is tracked by [dotnet/roslyn#82226](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/82226).

Roslyn already has a solution-wide rebuild and restart calculation for projects represented in its `Solution`. [`EmitSolutionUpdateResults.GetProjectsToRebuildAndRestart`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/src/Features/Core/Portable/EditAndContinue/EmitSolutionUpdateResults.cs) computes a fixed point across updated projects, projects with rude edits, project references, and running applications. It is not yet established that this implementation can directly consume results from an external F# provider. The current SDK prototype bypasses the unsupported-project result for F# and then performs a separate ancestor walk. I do not think that logic should be duplicated in `dotnet-watch` or in the F# compiler.

On the F# side, [dotnet/fsharp#20030](https://github.com/dotnet/fsharp/pull/20030) provides an experimental `FSharpHotReloadSession` with per-project baselines and a session-wide lifecycle:

- `AddProject`
- `EmitDelta`
- `Commit`
- `Discard`
- capability updates
- active-statement updates
- session disposal

That is the compiler engine the provider can wrap. It should not require a host to reproduce FCS workspace and session behavior.

The .NET project system already keeps process launch, runtime capability negotiation, delta application, rebuild, and restart separate from language compilation. Its current structure is documented in the [Hot Reload architecture document](https://github.com/dotnet/project-system/blob/main/docs/hot-reload-architecture.md), and the project-level implementation is shared between Visual Studio and Dev Kit.

## Proposed layering

My preferred direction is a language-provider contract in the shared managed Hot Reload path, rather than a second coordinator inside `dotnet-watch`.

```text
dotnet-watch / Visual Studio / C# Dev Kit in VS Code
                         |
             shared Hot Reload coordinator
                    /             \
          Roslyn provider       F# provider
                                from dotnet/fsharp
                                      |
                          FSharpHotReloadSession
```

The shared coordinator would continue to own:

- the host session lifecycle
- the set of running project instances
- runtime capabilities and break-state changes
- the complete project graph
- collection of updates and diagnostics from every language provider
- the rebuild, redeploy, and restart calculation
- the final apply plan
- coordinated commit or discard

Roslyn would continue to handle C# and Visual Basic through its existing implementation. The F# provider would be built and packaged from `dotnet/fsharp`, versioned with the F# compiler in the SDK or IDE, and would own:

- construction and maintenance of F# project snapshots
- the `FSharpWorkspace` and `FSharpChecker` lifetime
- F# session creation and project baseline capture
- F# change detection and compilation
- rude-edit and compilation diagnostics
- delta generation and conversion to the shared managed-update shape
- F# pending baseline commit and discard

The SDK should not load FCS through reflection or probe for individual FCS methods. It should reference a package with a strongly typed implementation of the agreed contract. Package naming and exact distribution are intentionally left open here.

## Provider contract

I think the provider contract should be language-neutral and should not require other compilers to implement Roslyn syntax, symbol, or `Compilation` abstractions.

The SDK prototype identifies a project instance by project file path and target framework. That may be sufficient for its current tests, but the shared contract should not assume it is sufficient across hosts. The same project can be built for multiple configurations, platforms, runtime identifiers, and output modules. The contract needs to distinguish:

- a host or provider project identity
- the evaluated build instance, including target framework and other relevant dimensions
- the runtime module identity, including output path and baseline MVID

The runtime-facing managed update shape already covers most of the runtime-facing data:

- module ID and module name
- metadata, IL, and PDB deltas
- updated types and methods
- required runtime capabilities
- sequence-point, active-statement, and exception-region updates

Provider and project identity should travel alongside that payload as coordinator metadata rather than being conflated with the runtime update itself.

The provider seam still needs to cover:

- session start and end
- project graph or project snapshot changes
- optional `HasChanges` checks
- capability changes
- entering and leaving break state
- active statements for provider-owned modules
- preparing an update without advancing committed baselines
- structured compilation and rude-edit diagnostics
- direct rebuild, redeploy, or restart requirements
- commit and discard after the host decides what was applied

The provider should report direct effects for the projects and runtime modules it owns. It should not independently calculate every running ancestor that needs to restart. The coordinator should combine provider-neutral results and run one solution-wide graph calculation. Reusing or extending Roslyn's current algorithm is preferable if its inputs can be generalized without changing existing C# and Visual Basic behavior.

When no compatible F# provider is available, the host should preserve its non-Roslyn rebuild-and-restart fallback. Current Roslyn main contains generic unsupported-project handling for this case, but the expected fallback must also be validated against the actual Roslyn package consumed by each SDK or IDE host. A missing provider must not terminate the Hot Reload session or prevent C# Hot Reload from continuing where it otherwise could.

## Project snapshots

The main unresolved input question is how the F# provider obtains complete, current project snapshots in each host.

The generic Roslyn project representation now contains documents, references, output information, and graph edges. FCS also needs ordered source files and the actual F# compiler arguments and tracked inputs. The SDK prototype currently obtains `FscCommandLineArgs` from the evaluated MSBuild graph and constructs an `FSharpWorkspace` through reflection.

The Visual Studio F# language service already maintains FCS project state and should not independently crack the same project again for Hot Reload. For a VS Code host such as C# Dev Kit, the design first needs to identify an actual source of F# project state. It should not assume that every VS Code installation already has a compatible F# language-service workspace.

One option is a second, F#-owned snapshot-source contract with host adapters. Another is to pass a normalized project description containing all compiler inputs. I would like input from the F# language service, project-system, and Roslyn maintainers before choosing between those.

Whatever the shape is, it should avoid three hosts maintaining separate copies of F# project cracking and should preserve source-file order, target framework identity, compiler options, project references, resources, signing inputs, and other tracked files.

## Mixed project graphs and transactions

A mixed update needs to be treated as one preparation cycle.

1. Each provider prepares updates and diagnostics without advancing its committed baseline.
2. The coordinator combines the results.
3. The coordinator determines which updates can be applied and which projects need rebuild or restart across the complete graph.
4. The host applies the resulting batch or initiates the required rebuild and restart operations.
5. Providers commit or discard their pending state consistently with the result.

This is important in both directions. A C# application may reference an F# library, and an F# application may reference a C# library. An edit in a library may affect several running applications of either language.

This coordination can make preparation and baseline advancement transactional, but it must not claim that runtime application itself is atomic. If the runtime applies one module update and then rejects another, the first update cannot necessarily be rolled back. The contract therefore needs to define:

- deterministic module application order
- how the host reports success or failure for each prepared update
- when each provider advances its committed baseline
- how providers recover after partial runtime application
- when the safe recovery is rebuild and restart

A provider must never advance its baseline for an update that the host did not confirm as applied. It also cannot simply discard a pending update whose module was already applied, since that would leave its baseline behind the running process.

The contract also needs an explicit answer for a cycle containing an applicable update in one independent graph and a rude edit in another. Before selecting a policy, the design should document current Roslyn behavior for that case and decide whether provider coordination preserves it. It should not assume that every provider must restart or discard unconditionally.

Compilation errors are different from rude edits. If one provider reports a blocking compilation error after another provider has prepared a delta, no provider may advance a baseline for an update the host did not apply. Whether an update in a genuinely independent graph may still proceed is a coordinator policy that should be pinned against current Roslyn behavior.

## Local prototype validation

I ran a local black-box matrix before writing this proposal. The current SDK main baseline was `aa2ca0b5160b`, and the prototype was tested at the exact #55128 head, `227e1dfce0b8`, with the matching F# compiler branch.

On current main:

- An F# library edit under a running C# application was detected, reported ENC1009 because F# does not support Hot Reload on that path, and restarted the process.
- A C# library edit under a running F# application applied in place through Roslyn.
- Coalesced C# and F# edits restarted because of the unsupported F# edit.

On the prototype:

- Both reference directions applied in place with the same process and preserved application state.
- Coalesced C# and F# edits were sent in one update batch with two module IDs and applied without restart.
- When the C# edit was applicable but the F# edit had a blocking compilation error, no update batch was sent. After the F# error was fixed, both edits were applied together without restart.

This is useful evidence for the coordinator requirements, but it is not a substitute for checked-in tests or proof that the current SDK-specific boundary is the right shared design. The local test asset and assertions remain on unpushed research branches for now.

## Tests to write first

I would start with fake-provider tests against the shared coordinator. They should be written before the implementation and should demonstrate the current gap or fail against the first incomplete contract before any fix is accepted.

| Scenario | Expected result |
| --- | --- |
| F# application, applicable method-body edit | One F# update is applied and committed without restart |
| C# application references an F# library, applicable F# edit | The library update is applied to the running C# application without restart |
| F# application references a C# library, applicable C# edit | The Roslyn update is applied without restarting the F# application |
| Applicable C# and F# edits in the same cycle | Both providers prepare before application; each advances its baseline only after the host confirms its corresponding module update was applied |
| C# compilation error after F# prepares an update in the same affected graph | The F# baseline does not advance unless its update is deliberately applied under a documented independent-graph policy |
| F# compilation error after Roslyn prepares an update in the same affected graph | The Roslyn baseline does not advance unless its update is deliberately applied under a documented independent-graph policy |
| Runtime applies one provider update and rejects the next | The coordinator reports the partial result, advances no unapplied baseline, does not discard state for an already-applied module, and follows the defined restart or resynchronization path |
| Rude edit in an F# library referenced by C# and F# applications | Every affected running ancestor is selected for rebuild and restart once |
| Applicable update in one graph and rude edit in an independent graph | The result follows the existing Roslyn fixed-point rules and does not restart unrelated processes |
| Provider missing or incompatible | F# edits use the current rebuild-and-restart fallback; C# Hot Reload continues to work |
| Same project path targeting multiple frameworks | Updates and restarts are associated with the correct target-framework instance |
| Same path and target framework with different configuration or runtime identifier | Each evaluated project instance and runtime module is associated with the correct provider state |
| Capabilities change after session start | Both providers classify the next edit using the current capabilities without recapturing baselines |
| Break state with active F# statements | Active statements are routed by module and F# reports either a valid remap or a structured rude edit |
| C# Razor or Blazor host references an F# library | C# and static-asset Hot Reload continue to work, and F# library edits follow the same mixed-graph rules |

The Razor or Blazor case is worth keeping as a regression test. [dotnet/sdk#28998](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/28998) documents a previous failure where merely referencing an F# project caused C# Hot Reload to fall back to a full rebuild.

After the contract tests, the initial integration matrix should run through command-line `dotnet-watch`. Visual Studio and C# Dev Kit should get their own integration coverage if and when those hosts adopt the provider.

## Possible implementation slices

I would expect the CLI work to be split into several PRs after the contract is agreed on.

1. Add failing coordinator tests with fake providers, then introduce the smallest language-neutral contract needed for `dotnet-watch` to make one update, rebuild, or restart decision. Keep existing C# and Visual Basic behavior unchanged.
2. Add the strongly typed F# provider package in `dotnet/fsharp`, wrapping `FSharpHotReloadSession` and the F# project snapshot source.
3. Replace the F# implementation in SDK #55128 with package registration and minimal CLI host wiring. Add the mixed `dotnet-watch` tests.
4. Remove the prototype reflection bridge and duplicated graph or transaction logic after the contract path is proven.
5. Treat Visual Studio and C# Dev Kit registration as later, separately reviewed work if those teams choose to adopt the provider.

The existing SDK PR can remain as prototype evidence while this is designed. Once the boundary is agreed on, I will modify it and potentially break it up rather than asking maintainers to review the current implementation as the final shape.

## Open questions

1. Should the provider contract and coordinator live in Roslyn Features, `Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.ExternalAccess.HotReload`, or a new neutral managed Hot Reload contracts package?
2. Should the F# provider be a new package, part of `FSharp.Compiler.Service`, or an assembly distributed in `Microsoft.FSharp.Compiler` alongside the SDK-matched FCS?
3. How should providers be discovered in `dotnet-watch`, Visual Studio, and C# Dev Kit without each host building a separate registration mechanism?
4. What is the shared project-snapshot contract, and which component supplies full F# compiler inputs in each host?
5. Can the existing Roslyn solution-wide commit and discard model directly coordinate external providers, or does the contract need a prepared-update token or per-project commit plan?
6. How should active statements be partitioned and routed to a provider that does not use Roslyn documents?
7. Is dotnet/roslyn#82226 a prerequisite for the Visual Studio provider path, or can the provider use the existing in-process F# workspace while the shared coordinator uses the generic project graph?
8. What compatibility policy should apply when the host contract and installed F# provider versions do not match?
9. What project-instance identity is stable across `dotnet-watch`, Visual Studio, and C# Dev Kit, and which dimensions belong in that identity rather than in runtime module identity?
10. What ordering and recovery guarantees can the host provide if runtime application succeeds for one module and fails for a later module in the same batch?
11. Should the neutral contract assembly be versioned separately from the F# implementation so hosts can load a provider without binding directly to the full FCS API surface?
12. Should the initial release remain preview-only behind the current F# compiler and SDK opt-ins until all three host paths are available?

## Related work

- [dotnet/sdk#55128](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/pull/55128)
- [dotnet/fsharp#19941](https://github.com/dotnet/fsharp/pull/19941)
- [dotnet/fsharp#11636](https://github.com/dotnet/fsharp/issues/11636)

Issues.Title: Replace nuget.org feed URLs with packagefeedproxy in tests
Issues.Body:
## Motivation

To reduce direct dependency on api.nuget.org in CI/PR pipelines, this PR migrates test infrastructure to use `https://packagefeedproxy.microsoft.io/nuget/v3/index.json` -- a controlled proxy that mirrors nuget.org through standard NuGet V3 protocol.

## Approach

**Simple URL swaps** for tests that use standard V3 feed operations (restore, install, package download via NuGet client protocol):

- `PackageManager.cs` - central `NuGetOrgFeed` constant used by many template integration tests
- `NuGetApiPackageManagerTests.cs` - additional sources array
- `TemplatePackagesTests.cs` - install request source URL and its assertion
- `DotnetNewInstallTests.cs` - `--nuget-source` / `--add-source` parameters (3 occurrences)
- `DotnetNewDetailsTest.Approval.cs` - inline NuGet.config and `--nuget-source` parameter
- `NuGetTests.cs` (TemplateDiscovery) - feed URL constant
- `analyzer_project/NuGet.config` - dotnet-format test asset
- Two `.verified.txt` approval files updated to match new expected output

**Protocol-compliant rewrite** for `GetLatestVersion()` which previously hardcoded the `api.nuget.org/v3-flatcontainer` endpoint directly. It now resolves the `PackageBaseAddress` resource from the V3 service index, following proper NuGet protocol and working with any compliant feed.

## What was NOT changed

- `NuGetInstallerTests.cs` - URLs are test data (metadata values parsed/validated), not network calls
- `AllCommonItemsCreate` approval files - these verify template OUTPUT (what users get from `dotnet new nugetconfig`), not test feeds
- `NugetSearchApiRequestTests.cs` - URL construction tests with no network calls
- `DotnetNewDetailsTest.CanDisplayDetails_RemotePackage_NuGetFeedWithVersion` - test is `[Ignore]`d

## Notes for reviewers

- The `.verified.txt` approval files may need regeneration if the proxy reports a different feed display name than expected. Running the affected tests and accepting new snapshots would fix this.
- The `GetLatestVersion` rewrite uses `StartsWith("PackageBaseAddress")` to match the resource type, handling versioned type strings like `PackageBaseAddress/3.0.0`.

Issues.Title: Make dotnet-watch test execution conditional in PR validation
Issues.Body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
The [SDK PR test filtering design](https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/blob/main/documentation/project-docs/pr-test-filtering.md) allows us to run fewer tests on PRs by only running suites when relevant paths change, while still running full coverage on CI (`main`/release). This is intended to reduce Helix consumption and improve PR turnaround without reducing safety on non-PR builds.

For motivation, I pulled a recent successful SDK PR validation run targeting `main` (**build 1524953 / PR 55453**) and measured watch-related Helix work item duration across all legs. The cumulative wall-clock compute for watch-related tests in that run was **31m 38s** (about **31.6 minutes**).  
Notable contributors in that run were:
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Watch.BrowserRefresh.Tests*`
- `Microsoft.DotNet.HotReload.Watch.Aspire.Tests*`

### Describe the solution you'd like
Adopt conditional PR test filtering for the dotnet-watch test surface so these tests run only when watch-related trigger paths change, while preserving full execution on non-PR CI builds.

This proposal follows the existing PR test-filtering design and uses declarative scope configuration as the source of truth.

Related to https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/55203

Issues.Title: Fix 'dotnet publish -o .' excluding all source files (CS5001)
Issues.Body:
Fixes #55295

## Problem

`dotnet publish -o .` (also `-o ./` and `-o ../<projname>`) fails with `CSC error CS5001: Program does not contain a static 'Main' method` for projects with top-level statements (and silently produces an empty assembly otherwise). This is a regression of #53626 whose fix (#53923, merged April) is present in `main` but ineffective for the value the CLI actually forwards — so the customer is correct that it still repros in 11.0 preview 6 / `main`.

## Root cause

The `$(PublishDir)/**` exclusion added to `DefaultItemExcludes` excludes every source file when the publish directory equals the project directory. #53923 added a guard to skip the exclusion in that case, but it used `[MSBuild]::NormalizePath`, which **preserves the input's trailing slash**:

| Expression | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `NormalizePath(projDir)` | `...\proj` (no slash) |
| `NormalizePath(projDir, '<absProjDir>\')` | `...\proj\` (trailing slash) → **not equal → guard fails** |

The CLI **always** forwards `PublishDir` as an absolute path **with** a trailing separator (`OptionExtensions.ForwardAsOutputPath` → `GetFullPath` + append `Path.DirectorySeparatorChar`). So the guard compared `C:\proj\` against `C:\proj`, found them unequal, and re-applied the exclusion → all source excluded → CS5001.

The #53923 regression test only set `PublishDir=.\` (relative), which never simulated the absolute-trailing-slash value the CLI emits, so it gave false confidence.

## Fix

Use `[MSBuild]::NormalizeDirectory` on **both** operands. It always emits a consistent trailing slash, so equal directories compare equal regardless of the input's trailing slash, while real publish subdirectories still differ and remain correctly excluded:

| Expression | Result | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NormalizeDirectory(projDir, '<absProjDir>\')` | `...\proj\` → equal | correctly **not** excluded |
| `NormalizeDirectory(projDir, './out/')` | `...\proj\out\` → differs | correctly excluded |

`NormalizeDirectory` is already widely used in SDK targets, so no new dependency/risk. A comment was added explaining why `NormalizeDirectory` (not `NormalizePath`) is required, to prevent a future regression.

## Test

Strengthened `It_does_not_exclude_source_files_when_publish_dir_is_project_root` to set `PublishDir` to `$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\` — the absolute trailing-slash value the CLI actually forwards — which is the case that regressed. The existing `It_excludes_items_in_publish_directory` test continues to guard the real-subdirectory case.

## Validation

- Full `build.cmd -c Debug` succeeds.
- All 22 tests in `GivenThereAreDefaultItems` pass against the built SDK, including both the root-dir (not excluded) and subdir (excluded) cases.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Fix 'dotnet publish -o .' excluding all source files (CS5001)" (#55461)

Issues.Title: Skip test-runtime install on cross-architecture builds
Issues.Body:
## Summary

On cross-build CI legs (e.g. x64 host building for arm64), the restore scripts install target-architecture runtimes into the host `.dotnet` folder. This causes `libhostpolicy` load failures when the NuGet credential provider resolves a shared framework built for the wrong CPU architecture, breaking `dotnet tool restore`.

## Fix

Skip installing test runtimes entirely when `TARGET_ARCHITECTURE` differs from the host architecture (since the built product won't run on the build machine anyway). Preserves the macOS Rosetta 2 exception where x64 binaries can run on arm64.

Port of the fix from `release/dnup` (PR #55435 by @dsplaisted) to `main`.

Fixes #55457

Issues.Title: Implement global command-line options for dotnet test (MTP): --timeout and --maximum-failed-tests
Issues.Body:
Implements the remaining "global" (run-level) command-line options for `dotnet test` under Microsoft.Testing.Platform, as requested in #49709. Options placed **before** `--` are treated as global and apply to the whole run; options **after** `--` continue to be forwarded per test application.

## New global options
- `--timeout <duration>` — aborts the run if total test-application execution time exceeds the given duration (e.g. `90s`, `5m`, `100ms`). Timing starts when the first test app begins and only accrues while at least one app is running. On timeout the run returns **`TestSessionAborted` (exit code 3)**, matching native MTP behavior.
- `--maximum-failed-tests <n>` — stops the run once the number of failed/errored/timed-out/cancelled test results reaches `n`, returning **exit code 13** (`TestExecutionStoppedForMaxFailedTests`). Counting is independent of retry bookkeeping.

## How cancellation works
The SDK now advertises a `ServerControlPipeName` capability in the handshake reply and opens a reverse control pipe. When a run-level policy trips, the SDK sends a cooperative `CancelSession` message to each test app over that pipe (the TestFx side landed in microsoft/testfx#9549). This requires the MTP 2.4 line, so `MicrosoftTestingPlatformPackageVersion` is bumped from 2.3.0 to 2.4.0-preview.

## Key changes
- New run-level coordinator `TestRunPolicy` (thread-safe timeout + max-failure state machine).
- New IPC contract: `ServerControlMessage` / `WaitForServerControlRequest` models + serializers, field ids, and registration.
- `TestApplication` / `TestApplicationActionQueue` / `TestApplicationHandler` wire the policy, reverse control pipe, and linked cancellation.
- Option definitions, validation, help text, and localization (`.resx` + `.xlf`).

## Tests
- `TestRunPolicyTests` (8, incl. a concurrency regression test for the timeout race), `ServerControlMessageSerializerTests` (3), `TestApplicationHandlerTests` (19), `TestCommandDefinitionTests` incl. new global-option parsing/validation cases (66).
- End-to-end in `GivenDotnetTestBuildsAndRunsTests`: `RunMTPSolutionWithMaximumFailedTestsReturnsPolicyExitCode` (exit 13) and `RunMTPProjectWithGlobalTimeoutReturnsTestSessionAborted` (exit 3).

Fixes #49709.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open PR "Implement global command-line options for dotnet test (MTP): --timeout and --maximum-failed-tests" (#55458)

Issues.Title: Official CI arm64 jobs failing with CredentialProvider.Microsoft.dll plugin startup errors
Issues.Body:
### Describe the bug
The internal SDK official CI pipeline has been failing on arm64 build legs for some time during restore/tool-restore with NuGet credential provider startup errors.

Observed example build:
https://dev.azure.com/dnceng/internal/_build/results?buildId=3030588

### To Reproduce
Run the internal official CI pipeline on `main` and inspect the failing arm64 jobs:
- `Mac arm64`
- `Linux arm64`

### Exceptions (if any)
Mac arm64:
`EXEC : Failed to load ... libhostpolicy.dylib ... incompatible architecture ...`
`[NuGet Manager] [Error] Problem starting the plugin ''.../CredentialProvider.Microsoft/CredentialProvider.Microsoft.dll''. Pipe is broken.`
`... Tools.proj(29,5): error MSB3077 ... dotnet tool restore ... ExitCode was set to -1.`

Linux arm64:
`EXEC : Failed to load ... libhostpolicy.so ... cannot open shared object file ...`
`[NuGet Manager] [Error] Problem starting the plugin ''.../CredentialProvider.Microsoft/CredentialProvider.Microsoft.dll''. Pipe is broken.`
`... Tools.proj(29,5): error MSB3077 ... dotnet tool restore ... ExitCode was set to -1.`

### Further technical details
- Pipeline: `dotnet-sdk-official-ci`
- Branch: `main`
- PR validation pipelines pass while this official CI pipeline fails.

Issues.Title: Backport Helix Monitor support to 10.0
Issues.Body:
Depends on https://github.com/dotnet/arcade/issues/17184

The Helix Monitor have proven its usefulness within the SDK repo.  The primary benefit is when an intermittent test failure occurs, rerun will re-queue the failing tests and run nothing else.  The secondary benefit is the build agent compute savings.

Issues.Title: Add optional Windows Explorer context menu for file-based apps
Issues.Body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

No specific problem.

This is an enhancement request to improve the Windows experience for .NET file-based apps and make the feature easier to discover.

### Describe the solution you'd like

.NET 10 File-based Apps are great for scripts and small utilities.

On Windows, it would be convenient if installing the .NET SDK could optionally register a context menu such as:

Run with .NET

Publish with .NET

This would avoid changing the default .cs file association (which many users expect to open in an editor), while still making file-based apps much easier to discover and use from Windows Explorer.

The context menu could be installed as an optional SDK feature.

### Alternatives you've considered

Currently, the only option is to open a terminal and run:

dotnet app.cs

Users can also manually create a custom launcher or modify file associations, but these require additional setup and are not discoverable for most users.

_No response_
